So I carried out that job as the on-duty investigative judge who was on duty that week. I wasn't in charge of the case. So the question would need to be put to the investigating judge who was supposed to actually be processing that case and who issued that order to the prosecutor's office.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now, the order was issued by you to the police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, and it had to be done in summary procedure due to the fact that the perpetrator fled from the scene of the crime. I was not the one who actually conducted the investigation. I was the investigating judge on duty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before you continue, Mr. Traldi. Witness, I would like to briefly re-visit what you said before the break. You said: "There must be a translation error because I only issued a wanted circular for an NN perpetrator and I did not say that I made a decision on initiating the investigation proceedings." You said that must be a translation error. You remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's not. It's not common in this court that you blame others for what is your own shortcoming. Both in the B/C/S version and in the English version the same text appears. Now, if you think it's wrong then you should have carefully read your statement and you should have corrected it instead of blaming translators for that. And this is now the third time that a similar thing happens.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm not seeking comment at this moment, although apologies are -- I understand that you want to apologise for that. I was explaining to you that it's now the third time that you're not appropriately dealing with your own statement. The other one was your knowledge about what happened to a case. You had gained knowledge in the Karadzic case, nevertheless in the Mladic case your statement says that you do not know what happened where you now do know. You explained that by saying that you considered it irrelevant. And I now take you to the third item, the third item deals with the examples of the cases which demonstrate -- which demonstrate how well the system was performing its duties in paragraph 27. Questions were put to you by Mr. Traldi on whether really these cases were about Croat and Muslim victims, at least nuances are to be made there because a company is not a Croat or a Muslim and you explained that since it was in the area mainly inhabited by that you just put them on the same level. We heard from Mr. Stojanovic in your absence, I think, that he had discussed with you that the examples given in paragraphs 27 are not giving full and adequate support to your statement, and also that he discussed that with you. Under those circumstances, you should have corrected your statement. These are just three examples of where you have been inaccurate and one time even blaming others for your own inaccuracy. That's not what we expect a witness to do and it's also not what we expect a witness to do who has a professional background which should him make aware of these matters. I leave it to that but I urge you to be very accurate and very precise in any answers. And if there are any other corrections to be made to your statement, it would be preferable that you do it on your own initiative rather than that the matter is put to you in cross-examination or during questions by the Bench. I leave it to that. Mr. Traldi, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir, we discussed Batkovic camp before the break. Several of the senior officers at Batkovic camp, Major Djoko Pajic, Petar Dmitrovic, Ljubisa Misic, and Djordje Krstic, are currently on trial in Bijeljina for crimes committed at Batkovic; right?

utterances.speaker: SAVO BOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: None of them were tried in your court during the war, were they?

utterances.speaker: SAVO BOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Finally, sir, I have a few brief questions about Bijeljina. You lived in Bijeljina municipality throughout the war; right?

utterances.speaker: SAVO BOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, you don't mention this in your statement, but the overwhelming majority of the Muslim population of Bijeljina left the municipality during the war between 1992 and 1995; right?

utterances.speaker: SAVO BOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I'm going to ask Ms. Stewart to play a video-clip labelled 65 ter 22668A and we'll have to play it twice.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "This is one of the many new admission centres in Tuzla, last night one hour before midnight following the 1400 expelled Bosniaks from Semberija who were accommodated in other admission centres in Tuzla and the neighbouring towns yesterday, soon this hall will be prepared to admit new victims who will come in the course of the night from Mount Majevica area. It is midnight. Bus after bus is arriving to Tuzla during this rain and chilly night. Those who are coming are women, children, old people, and only now and then an able-bodied man. Others have been separated from their families by Chetnik gangs, imprisoned in camps. There are Bosniak families arriving, who were once well off but now all their property has been seized and looted and who even had to pay a lot in foreign currency and gold for deportation tickets for a night walk in rain and through Majevica woods, past minefields. "Even seriously disabled, poor old grannies, and paralyzed Munevera Bajramovic. Hopefully at least someone in this dormant world will ask to whom could have Munevera Bajramovic posed an impediment, same as Zade Manjic's twins also from Janja. They don't even have names yet, they're just born, yet these days the brother and sister from the Manjic family will get border passes and number for toddlers. "Lord, may Bosnia -- may justice in Bosnia win out at least. These people are not handball or basketball game spectators. These people are expelled Bosniaks from Janja waiting for mattresses and sponges to be put on the hall floor, the ill-fate and constant companions of Bosniaks in the current days of horrible genocide committed against them by Chetnik military leaders from Pale. "People are waiting. Another Tuzla admission centre hall is slowly getting filled up. The second hour past midnight is passing. This night another 427 expellees have arrived from Semberija. The people with harsh scars on their souls, physically and emotionally broken. The only thing that criminals did not manage to kill in them is hope. They are getting ready to at least spend peacefully their second night in exile. The first night they spent surrounded by gangs of Vojkan Djurkovic, Rista, and other war criminals in the trucks on Majevica mountain. It is the 19th of September of the war 1994, in Tuzla, one hour past noon, yet another bus from Majevica and yet another group of Bosniak expellees. The Janja tragedy is getting to an end. Now it's the turn for final ethnic cleansing of Bijeljina while the world is still talking about the dictators from Haiti. "

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir, the people we saw in that video who'd been sent out of Bijeljina, those were clearly civilians; right.

utterances.speaker: SAVO BOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: You're aware that as described in that video, Muslims were expelled from Bijeljina in September 1994; right?

utterances.speaker: SAVO BOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: By the end of the war there were few -- very few Muslims left in Bijeljina municipality; right?

utterances.speaker: SAVO BOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honours, I tender 65 ter 22668A and I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I see that the CD is on its way to Madam Registrar. Having now received the CD, Madam Registrar, the number to be assigned to the video played?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 22668A receives number P6899, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P6899 is admitted into evidence. Mr. Stojanovic, any need to re-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just need a little time, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bojanovic, can you please tell us if the directives for criminal prosecution ever order how to try crimes -- property crimes, theft, aggravated theft, and crimes like that?

utterances.speaker: SAVO BOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't understand what you asked me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm going to simplify the question. Did you ever have any instructions as to how and what sentence should be given for property crimes, theft, aggravated theft, and so on?

utterances.speaker: SAVO BOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We didn't have any instructions because the Trial Chamber presiding judges would take their position accordingly, because there were a lot of such crimes cropping up during the war. So we took the position, as I said in my statement, that we should try such crimes regardless of who the perpetrators were. But we took the common position precisely due to the fact that some perpetrators were from the Army of Republika Srpska. So we would pass -- hand down suspended sentences in those cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Is it your experience that this practice regarding sentencing policy was something that was followed before the war also?

utterances.speaker: SAVO BOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you remember what the practice was in peacetime for prosecution of theft?

utterances.speaker: SAVO BOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that the practice was similar when we're talking about sentencing policy that we applied in trying cases with such crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you recall if there were any cases when you handed down executive sentences?

utterances.speaker: SAVO BOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was the practice as well. I did mention that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please look at P6896.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we do so, could I ask you a few additional questions. You said irrespective of background we would try persons the same way. You also explained that the reason for giving suspended sentences was that the -- it would be good for the army so that the performance of the army would be strengthened. Now, first of all, would you send a Bosniak or a Muslim -- would you have only a suspended sentence for him because he could then strengthen the capacity of the VRS? I'm trying to understand the logic in your answers.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course. We would hand down the same sentence if a Bosniak had committed the same kind of sentence -- a crime, suspended sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Also in order to allow him to go back to his VRS units?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Or --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat what he said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you repeat what you last said.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because there were Muslims in the Army of Republika Srpska, at least those that were stationed in Bijeljina. There were two battalions made up of Muslims. I think this was in the 3rd Majevica Brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What time-period are you talking about at this moment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The whole war time period.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Do you have one example of a Muslim being -- receiving a suspended sentence in order to be able to return to his unit in a theft case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We did not have such a case, at least I'm not aware of one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So it's all theoretical rather than anything else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to draw your attention to something if you would allow me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would like to first ask my next question and then I give you an opportunity to draw my attention to whatever you consider important. You explained that you gave these suspended sentences out of concern for the functioning of the VRS. Did I understand that well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, was the well functioning of the VRS more important than doing justice to victims?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, we tried to strike a balance between the two, the need to act fairly, to administer justice, and to have the VRS function because of the war that we happened to be in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, is that one of the accepted purposes for punishment to be treated more leniently because the army needs you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it couldn't be put that way. But at first when the war started that was more pronounced and I think that we deterred potential perpetrators that way, and later on in 1993 and 1994 we had less such situations. That's what I wanted to tell you a moment ago, that through this deterrence we managed to have less crime of that kind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do I understand you well that sending them back to the units was more deterring than to give them sentence which they would have to serve in jail?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it could be put that way because there was no case when a suspended sentence was actually annulled, or rather, that the person in question had committed another crime during the suspended sentence period.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for those answers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I have a slightly different question. Sir, at page 57, line 12, Mr. Stojanovic asked you: "Is it your experience that this practice regarding sentencing policy was something that was followed before the war also?" You answered: "Yes." The next question was: "Can you remember what the practice was in peacetime for prosecution of theft?" You said: "I think the practice was similar when we are talking about sentencing policy and we applied in trying cases with such crimes." Now, my question to you is you said -- told us that you as the judges decided during the war that in order not to undermine the strength of the army you're going to put this practice in place. My question to you is: What was the reason for the similar policy in peacetime? There was no army to be strengthened; what was the reason for it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, from this point of view it's hard to answer that question now, but I assume -- well, I don't have that experience now, but I believe that even now the ordinary crime of theft is dealt with by way of suspended sentences. I really haven't had the opportunity to check that, but as far as ordinary theft is concerned I think that that is the case. Aggravated theft is different, a different kind of sentence is imposed in such cases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May I ask the question: Am I supposed to understand that you are saying in the entire history of former Yugoslavia to date crimes of theft have never been punished by a jail sentence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So there has been jail sentences for theft?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What underpinned the policy of suspended sentences in peacetime? You said it is difficult to answer that question. Is it then the truth not that in fact that policy didn't exist at that time? You've just told us that there were jail sentences?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course there were but it depends on the positions taken in the courts and they were different.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sir, you've got to make up your mind which is correct. You can't say there was a policy of sentencing people only on suspended sentences when you also admit that there were cases where people were given jail sentences for theft.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it all depended on the specific case, on the circumstances under which a crime was committed. I didn't say always. I said that there were cases of suspended sentences.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You have given me the same answer that you have just given me and I asked you a question. You cannot say there was a policy of giving suspended sentences for theft if, in fact, there were cases of jail sentences. It must mean that in peacetime cases were dealt with according to their merit, a suspended sentence was given when it was found appropriate and a jail sentence was given when it was found appropriate. Is it not so? That's why you say it depended on circumstances. So the judiciary was independent and exercising its discretion judicially, not because of military reasons. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. I'm done, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I ask for P6896 in e-court. That is the judgement that we saw during the prosecutor's cross-examination. In the English version could we have the next page, please. And then in the English version the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bojanovic, the crime of aggravated theft, paragraph 3 of Article 148, this person, Dusan Arsenic, did he receive a suspended sentence or not?

utterances.speaker: SAVO BOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was sentenced to prison one year, three months.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Does this judgement confirm that in certain cases, even during the war, you gave jail sentences for certain property-related crimes?

utterances.speaker: SAVO BOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. I've already said it depends on the circumstances involved, and this case shows that. I believe that this is not the only jail sentence for this kind of crime.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know what the position was of the superior commands in respect of the protection of property that had been abandoned at that point in time by the owners?

utterances.speaker: SAVO BOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, certainly, that's what we read in one of the judgements that we saw here, that the commands of units strictly asked their members to refrain from theft and they welcomed these judgements of ours because at first in particular they were flooded with complaints against the members of their units.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I just want to intervene here, Mr. Stojanovic. Sir, when I asked you questions you made a distinction between theft and aggravated theft, and you did say that it was a -- the policy to give suspended sentences for theft but not for aggravated theft. Is that not so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now, this case that you are being referred to, is it theft or aggravated theft? Just look at that paragraph.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is the crime of aggravated theft under Article 148. That is what you can see here. You can see it in the statement of reasons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Therefore, it is not a case of theft that was under your policy of suspended sentences?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, this is aggravated theft.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So this does not prove anything? It doesn't disprove your policy?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not quite understand you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Your policy was that theft is punished by suspended sentences. Aggravated theft was punished by anything that was appropriate during war time. So this does not detract from your policy, this case does not detract from your policy because this is not theft, this is aggravated theft?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bojanovic, in the criminal law that you applied, was there a difference in terms of punishment for theft mentioned in Article 147 and aggravated theft mentioned in paragraph 148?

utterances.speaker: SAVO BOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a difference. I haven't seen the law in a long time. I cannot say specifically but there was a difference in terms of the punishment envisaged.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please tell the Trial Chamber - and this is going to be my last question - how did you organise the duty rosters of investigative judges in terms of time in the military court?

utterances.speaker: SAVO BOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At first there were three of us judges there. We would be on duty ten days per month. After the number of judges was increased, then we took turns on a weekly basis. There were quite a few cases, especially in the beginning of the war. It was really hard work, very strenuous. Sometimes we would even carry out three on-site investigations in a single day.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bojanovic. Thank you very much for the answers you have provided.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stojanovic. Any further questions, Mr. Traldi?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Just very briefly, Mr. President. Further the cross-examination by Mr. Traldi:

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, regarding the case we're looking at, the Arsenic case, do you have any personal knowledge as to how much time if any he spent in prison?

utterances.speaker: SAVO BOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honours, it turns out I only had one question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Traldi. Let me just -- give me a minute to think about something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I have here you were asked questions about Cvetkovic and Jurosevic and you said: Since the suspects were not military personnel as we established through further investigative activities the case was transferred due to the lack of jurisdiction. Now, it was put to you that at least during the crime of murder that there were military personnel. How do you reconcile establishing that they were not and what we find in the document that was shown to you that his military post was specifically mentioned? Was that a mistake in your statement or was it -- what was it?

utterances.speaker: SAVO BOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At first when the war started in Bosnia in addition to the regular army there were many paramilitary formations, not to enumerate all of them, there were quite a few of them, and one of these paramilitary formations were some volunteers from Serbia and these two accused persons belonged to them. At first when the military court started operating the position was taken that military courts should try all crimes perpetrated by physical persons because there was an imminent threat of war that had been declared and all able-bodied men of military age were potential perpetrators who fell under military courts. It was only in the beginning of 1993 that the position was taken that only perpetrators of crimes who were members of the VRS who had committed a crime while they were in the army while they were conducting their military duties fell under military courts. That's what the Law on Military Courts and the military prosecutor's office said. I think it was in 1993 when I was no longer at the court. That was the practice at first, I mean when jurisdiction was not exactly delineated. So we dealt with all persons including Cvetkovic and Jurosevic. To the best of my knowledge --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me then interrupt you there because in your statement you say the case was transferred due to the lack of jurisdiction to the regular judicial authorities in Brcko where the crime had been committed. That sounds as if the case was not referred to the military courts or the military prosecutor which you -- I think you just explained were the competent authorities. Or have I misunderstood you?

utterances.speaker: SAVO BOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You did not quite understand what I was saying. The case was not transferred to the regular court in Brcko then; it was later. We carried out an investigation. I as investigating judge did that. We already discussed it. I did certain things but it was only later - I don't know exactly when - I think it was even after the war that this case was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but what -- what did you do during the war? Because as I read paragraph 12 of your statement it doesn't say: After many, many years the case was transferred to the regular judicial authorities. It says: "I ordered detention, continued the investigation, since the suspects were not military personnel, as we established. The case was transferred due to the lack of jurisdiction to the regular judicial authorities." What did you do then during the war immediately after the crime was committed, if this is only after years and years?

utterances.speaker: SAVO BOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: SAVO BOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We have to take into account a particular fact. As far as I know during the war the judiciary in Brcko was not functioning at all. Brcko was directly at the front line. So the judiciary organs did not function at all in Brcko.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's fine, but what did you then do in late 1992/early 1993 with this case where you suggest that you sent it to the regular judicial authorities in Brcko and now you're explaining to us that you didn't because they were not functioning?

utterances.speaker: SAVO BOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I completed the investigation, I think that you have that among these documents that were submitted here as exhibits, and I returned the case to the military prosecutor's office. I don't know the exact date but it can be found here and it was returned to the prosecutor's office. I really don't know what the prosecutor's office did after I had completed the investigation. You would have to ask the military prosecutor's office for that information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So at least paragraph 12 of your statement is rather confusing because it doesn't say in any way that you sent the case to the military prosecutor's office. It says: "The case was transferred due to the lack of jurisdiction to the regular judicial authorities in Brcko ..." Without saying that that happened years after that and without saying that at the time you sent the case to the military prosecutor. You as a lawyer, you must have understood that this is not a very accurate way of describing the situation. Or could you explain why this is accurate in view of what you told us just a minute ago?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Perhaps we could have D747 on the screen again, paragraph 12 in both versions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please have a look at paragraph 12, especially the first paragraph -- or the first "linija," and tell me if you agree that it's rather confusing if not even misleading.

utterances.speaker: SAVO BOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree, you're right. A bit -- well, it's true, my statement is a bit imprecise and clumsy, but I have explained what it was all about and it can be checked. After the investigation was completed I referred the entire case along with all the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm at this moment more interested not in exactly what happened at the time but why you give a confusing picture of what happened instead of being accurate. And this is -- I think we dealt with three previous occasions, this is number 4. What happened on the 14th of July when you were interviewed? How was that interview conducted?

utterances.speaker: SAVO BOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, believe me, as it's been quite a while I was a bit imprecise in these statements of mine, but the essence is what I gave by way of a supplement to the statement, what I explained just now, and I don't see that this should now be taken as something that I had invented or added. It's just the fact that so much time has elapsed, over 20 years. I didn't remember all the details.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, you earlier blamed the translators, just to give one example. And Mr. Stojanovic told us a while ago that you had together discussed, this week I take it, that the other paragraph that the examples did not support your statement. So therefore, to say it was such a long time ago when the matter apparently was discussed this week and it was established that the documents did not support -- at least not fully support your statement, that is not explained by saying it was such a long time ago. Apart from that, my question was: How the interview was conducted in July of this year? What happened? How did it start? Who interviewed you?

utterances.speaker: SAVO BOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This man, Petrusic I think his name was, talked to me, and on the first page his exact name is recorded. I cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you have answered the question about Mr. Petrusic. Where did the interview take place?

utterances.speaker: SAVO BOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Bijeljina, in my office.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: How long did it last?

utterances.speaker: SAVO BOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, about two hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, were you asked questions anew or did you start -- did you take as a starting point your Karadzic statement?

utterances.speaker: SAVO BOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that statement was the starting point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Were you invited to make any corrections to that or were specific questions put to you in relation to that statement?

utterances.speaker: SAVO BOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we made some corrections then as we did when preparing this testimony during the proofing, but this really I missed it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's not an answer to my question. My question was whether you read it and said: Well, this should be corrected and that should be corrected or whether specific questions were put to you on matters you had not raised in -- by your own initiative?

utterances.speaker: SAVO BOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. The conversation did take place in the form of an interview, but the basis was the statement I gave in Radovan Karadzic's case and there were some mistakes that crept in like this one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But that one was not corrected?

utterances.speaker: SAVO BOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- one other question: All the documents you were commenting on, were they shown to you again in July or were they not shown to you again in July?

utterances.speaker: SAVO BOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they were not shown to me again. I didn't have the opportunity to look at them again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So the statement was given and was signed without you having reviewed again the documents which you -- did you see them when you were preparing for the Karadzic case?

utterances.speaker: SAVO BOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some of them I did, yes, but not all of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you tell me that documents you are commenting on in your statement, as given in the Karadzic case, that you had not seen all the documents when you gave that statement for the Karadzic case?

utterances.speaker: SAVO BOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw most of the documents when I testified before the Tribunal in the Karadzic case, especially for the cases that are referred to here. I did see those documents that were used as evidence --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters notes: Could the witness please repeat the names of the cases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the names of the cases is what the interpreters are asking.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Cvetkovic, Jurosevic, and Rado Mihajlovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But these documents, as you said, were not shown to you again in July of this year when you made this Mladic statement? Yes -- I saw you were nodding, but could you please say aloud what your answer is to that question. I asked you whether they were not shown to you again in the Mladic case and your answer is?

utterances.speaker: SAVO BOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they were not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for those answers. Have the questions by the Bench triggered the need for any further questions? If not, Mr. Bojanovic, this concludes your testimony in this court. I would like to thank you very much for coming a long way to The Hague and for having answered the questions that were put to you either by the parties or by the Bench and I wish you a safe return home again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll take a break. Is the Defence ready to call its next witness after the break?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, we are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then we'll resume at 20 minutes to 2.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom. I do understand that the parties have agreed in trying to see whether the testimony of the next witness can be concluded even today, and the Chamber is willing to add 15 minutes but due to our programmes it could not be much more than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I think Mr. Lukic and I will probably be able to work within that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's appreciated.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, I could introduce Ms. Caroline Edgerton who will be assisting with the cross-examination in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Welcome to court, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Kukobat. Before you give evidence the Rules require that you make a solemn declaration. The text is handed out to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated, Mr. Kukobat. Mr. Kukobat, you'll first be examined by Mr. Lukic. You find him to your left. Mr. Lukic is counsel for Mr. Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Mr. Kukobat.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KUKOBAT
utterances.text: Good day.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: For the transcript, would you please tell us your first and last name.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KUKOBAT
utterances.text: Dusan Kukobat.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It was recorded as my question -- ah, very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can we have 1D1715 on our screens, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kukobat, could you look at the right-hand screen once you put your glasses on and could you tell us if you see a document in front of you?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KUKOBAT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I want to ask you this first regarding the document: Did you provide the Defence of General Mladic with a statement?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KUKOBAT
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you see a signature on the screen?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KUKOBAT
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you recognise this signature?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KUKOBAT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Whose signature is it?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KUKOBAT
utterances.text: It's mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now look at the last page of the statement, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you see the signature on the screen?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KUKOBAT
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you recognise the signature?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KUKOBAT
utterances.text: Yes, it is my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is what you told the Defence of General Mladic correctly and accurately represented in the statement?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KUKOBAT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And what is recorded in the statement, is it truthful and correct according to your best recollection?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KUKOBAT
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If I were to put the same questions to you today, would you give the same answers?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KUKOBAT
utterances.text: Yes, I would.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, we would tender this statement into the evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D1715 receives number D757, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I will not have any questions for this witness. I will just read a very short statement summary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If you're confident that we would have sufficient time, otherwise you could even consider to read the summary where you have no other questions for a later stage, but if it is a short one please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's very short.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Dusan Kukobat will testify about the situation in the area of Kljuc municipality after August 1992 -- actually, after 19th of August 1992, when he served as the Chief of Staff of the brigade. He will testify about the fighting with the Muslim-Croat units in the Sana River valley, also at -- in Jajce war theatre. General Kukobat will testify about developments around Bihac safe zone and about attacks from Bihac safe zone on Serb positions. He will testify about actions of Croatian army in Bosnia. General Kukobat will confirm that Ratko Mladic always emphasised that no crimes were to be committed against the enemy and that the civilians and prisoners should be particularly protected. And at the end General Kukobat will testify about his contacts with General Mladic. That was short summary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Kukobat, no questions were asked, but of course we have read your statement so that is in evidence. You'll now be cross-examined by Mr. Traldi. You'll find him to your right, and Mr. Traldi is counsel for the Prosecution. Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KUKOBAT
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Can we have Exhibit P354, page 51 in the English and the B/C/S transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir, as this comes up it will be one of General Mladic's notebooks from the war. Sorry, it will take us just a minute to get the right page. So we see here General Mladic record a meeting with the Chief of Staff of the army of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia on the 12th of August, 1992. Turning to page 55 in both versions, we see that he records that he had a conversation with officers from BH with ranks major and colonel and that 66 officers were in attendance. Now, you mention in paragraph 4 of your statement a meeting with General Mladic and General Tolimir in Belgrade. What we see here refers to the meeting you attended; correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KUKOBAT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Below that it says: "Tomorrow at 1200 hours in the hall of the Guards Centre a meeting with officers ranked captain first class and lower." Were you aware that a meeting with lower-ranking officers was held on the next day?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KUKOBAT
utterances.text: No, I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: What is the guards centre building?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KUKOBAT
utterances.text: The meeting was not held at the guards centre building but in the conference hall or the meeting room at the army command of that military district at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And that's a Yugoslav army command; right?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KUKOBAT
utterances.text: The Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: How did you hear about this meeting?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KUKOBAT
utterances.text: I was informed by my superior. I'm not sure, but I received the notification along the line of command. I'm not quite sure how I got the invitation, but I did find out about the meeting. It's been a long time ago. I cannot recall that now.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Do you recall who your superior was at the time?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KUKOBAT
utterances.text: At the time I was the brigade Chief of Staff and the -- my superior was the commander of the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Do you recall his name?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KUKOBAT
utterances.text: I think that his name was Colonel Ratko Markovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Did General Mladic describe the VRS's goals at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KUKOBAT
utterances.text: Yes, he presented the situation in Bosnia and Herzegovina and explained the objectives of the fight of the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: When you say he explained the objectives, did he explain particular territories that the VRS was trying to achieve control over?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KUKOBAT
utterances.text: No, this was not discussed at that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: So what objectives did he identify, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KUKOBAT
utterances.text: I cannot remember exactly, but I think it was the protection of the Serbian people in territories where they were located, protection of property. That is in brief what I can recall now of what was discussed at that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: When you went to this meeting, you were a VJ officer and received your salary from the Yugoslav army; right?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KUKOBAT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: During your service in the VRS in Bosnia, did you continue to receive your salary from the VJ?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KUKOBAT
utterances.text: Yes, except for a short period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And specifically did you receive it through the 30th Personnel Centre?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KUKOBAT
utterances.text: Yes, the 30th Personnel Centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir, I want to turn now to some brief questions about your time in Kljuc. You became the 17th Light Infantry Brigade's Chief of Staff when you first arrived in Kljuc; right?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KUKOBAT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, it doesn't say this in your statement but you only remained in Kljuc for a few months; right?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KUKOBAT
utterances.text: Yes, until -- until mid-December 1992 I stayed at my post in that brigade, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: That's when you became a brigade commander in Petrovac; right?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KUKOBAT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: So I'm going to ask now about the structure of the 17th Brigade during your time in Kljuc. Your brigade was under the command of the 2nd Krajina Corps; right?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KUKOBAT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: The brigade commander was Drago Samardzija?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KUKOBAT
utterances.text: Yes, Samardzija was the brigade commander at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: As Chief of Staff you served as his deputy?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KUKOBAT
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And your brigade command would send daily reports to the corps command; right?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KUKOBAT
utterances.text: At the time that I was the Chief of Staff of the brigade, the brigade was resubordinated to the 1st Krajina Corps. It was actually part of the 30th Division and it was carrying out its assignment within the 30th Division of the 1st Krajina Corps and of course it received orders and received -- and sent reports to the division, and from time to time the corps command also wanted to be informed about the activities of the brigade at the front.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: How did the brigade staff compile information to include in those reports?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KUKOBAT
utterances.text: We had reports from the subordinate commanders of the units, of battalions, and of other subordinated units.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: When you became Chief of Staff, Bosko Lukic who had been the Chief of Staff until you arrived became the assistant commander for logistics; right?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KUKOBAT
utterances.text: I was told that he would be appointed logistics assistant commander but this was never put into practice. I don't know if there was a document on that appointment; however, I never met Mr. Lukic and another officer was carrying out the logistics officer duties. Then a third officer was appointed to the post after a certain period of time. So Major Lukic did not appear in the brigade. I don't know why not, what were the reasons that he did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Looking at the battalions of your brigade, the 1st Battalion was stationed in Sitnica; right? Are you having troubled receiving interpretation?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KUKOBAT
utterances.text: The interpreter is not sure about the name of the location that you mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: The 1st Battalion was in Sitnica, S-i-t-n-i-c-a; correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KUKOBAT
utterances.text: The battalions were along the front line facing Jajce. They were not in inhabited places. They were deployed according to the combat disposition at the time that I assumed the post of Chief of Staff of the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: The 1st Battalion's commander was Branko Ribic?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KUKOBAT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: The 2nd Battalion's commander was Jovo Kevac?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KUKOBAT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Mr. Ribic's deputy was Marko Adamovic; right?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KUKOBAT
utterances.text: No. Marko Adamovic was the assistant commander for morale and legal and religious affairs at the time that I assumed the post of Chief of Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Is that in the brigade?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KUKOBAT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Who commanded the 3rd Battalion?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KUKOBAT
utterances.text: Brane Volas. It's just that I'm not sure right now who was in command of the 1st, of the 2nd, and the 3rd Battalion, but the officers were the command -- in command of the battalions that we just referred to.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir, when you arrived in Kljuc you were aware many of the Muslims had already left; right?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KUKOBAT
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Did you become aware of that shortly after you arrived?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KUKOBAT
utterances.text: I didn't know anything about those events because I reported for duty in the field -- actually, at the front line that was outside of the inhabited places. So I did not spend any time in Kljuc except for the time that I passed through Kljuc in order to report to the brigade command.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Did Kljuc remain within your area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KUKOBAT
utterances.text: The area of responsibility was the zone at the front. Kljuc was not part of the brigade's area of responsibility during the time that I was at the post of Chief of Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: So you have in your evidence no information about what was happening there at the time at all, happening in Kljuc?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KUKOBAT
utterances.text: I didn't have any information at the time and it was not discussed at any time. The only thing I heard after the war from the media is what we all know anyway about the events, about what was happening or not happening. I really cannot talk about that. I was not an eye-witness to those events.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Several members of the brigade have been convicted or charged since the war for what happened in Kljuc, right, that's one of the things you've heard?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KUKOBAT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: That includes your commander, Drago Samardzija, who's currently under indictment?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KUKOBAT
utterances.text: I am aware of that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: It includes Bosko Lukic and Marko Adamovic who were recently convicted of war crimes in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KUKOBAT
utterances.text: I also am aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And it also includes Marko Samardzija, a company commander in the 2nd Battalion who was convicted in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN KUKOBAT
utterances.text: I don't know Marko Samardzija and I don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Traldi. Witness, since the Defence has no further questions for you either and the Chamber has no questions for you, this concludes your testimony in this court. As I said before, it was not only those questions but also the statement you've given to the Defence which is now evidence before this Court. I'd like to thank you very much and we are quite happy that you do not have to stay over the weekend and that you can travel home and we wish you a safe return home again. You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber appreciates the way in which the parties have dealt with the way of examination of this witness, which allowed him to return home before the weekend. We have six minutes left, but if there are no specific matters to be raised then we'll adjourn early. We adjourn for the day and we'll resume Monday, the 10th of November, in this same courtroom I at 9.30 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 10th day of November, 2014, at 9.30 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 2.08 p.m.,
